titleText.es: Dicen que no se puede argumentar contra los datos, ¿pero a qué viene esa actitud derrotista? Si le pones ganas, puedes argumentar contra CUALQUIER COSA.
titleText.en: They say you can't argue with results, but what kind of defeatist attitude is that? If you stick with it, you can argue with ANYTHING.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish and English texts are the exact title attributes from the Spanish archive and official xkcd. OCR omitted the standalone Y that begins the final paragraph of the speech and all five printed dollar signs on the money bags; those source-checked units are restored explicitly. OCR also dropped several written accents that remain visible in the raster.

regions.labelEs: POR MUCHO QUE OS DIGAN, NUNCA DEJÉIS DE COMPRAR LOTERÍA. HE FRACASADO MUCHAS VECES, PERO NUNCA ME HE RENDIDO. EMPECÉ A HACER TURNOS DOBLES PARA PODER PAGAR MÁS BILLETES DE LOTERÍA. Y AQUÍ ME VEIS, LA PRUEBA VIVIENTE DE QUE SI PERSEVERÁIS, TRIUNFARÉIS.

applications.explanationEn: Por mucho que opens the concession, and digan uses the special open-ended form for whatever people may say; os identifies the familiar group receiving those words.
Os marks the familiar plural listeners used with vosotros in Spain.
Nunca makes the instruction negative, and dejéis is the command form addressed to a familiar group.
The -éis ending is addressed to a familiar plural group in the Spain vosotros system.
Dejéis changes for the addressed group, de links it to comprar, and comprar stays in its unchanged -ar form.
He matches the speaker, and fracasado supplies the completed failure connected to the present story.
He matches the speaker, and rendido is the completed-action form; the preceding me belongs to rendirse, “to give up.”
Empecé gives the completed beginning, a links it to the activity, and hacer stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Hacer supplies the work action, and turnos names the scheduled work periods.
Dobles follows turnos in the neutral order for a descriptive adjective.
Dobles carries plural -es to match the plural noun turnos and has the same plural form for either gender.
Para introduces the purpose, and poder stays in its unchanged -er form.
Poder names the ability, and pagar remains in its unchanged -ar form.
Veis is the present form of ver for a familiar plural group in Spain.
Prueba names evidence, and viviente presents the speaker as a living embodiment of it.
Prueba names the claimed evidence, while de que introduces the claim supplied as its content; viviente describes that proof between them.
Si introduces the possible condition, perseveráis stays in an ordinary present form, and triunfaréis gives the future result.
The -áis ending marks an ordinary present action by a familiar plural group in Spain.
Triunfaréis keeps the complete verb triunfar and adds -éis for what the group will do.
The final -éis also identifies the familiar plural group addressed with vosotros.

regions.labelEs: TODAS LAS CHARLAS MOTIVADORAS DE GENTE CON ÉXITO DEBERÍAN AVISAR SOBRE EL SESGO DE SUPERVIVENCIA.

applications.explanationEn: Motivadoras follows charlas in the neutral descriptive order.
Motivadoras uses feminine plural -as to match charlas.
Con éxito forms the conventional expression describing a successful person or result.
Deberían gives a softened recommendation for the plural subject, and avisar stays in its unchanged -ar form.
Deberían keeps the full verb deber and adds the plural conditional ending -ían.
Sesgo names the distortion, and de supervivencia identifies it as the distortion created by seeing the surviving cases.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por mucho que
cards.noteEn: Por begins the concessive connector por mucho que, used to say that a result holds no matter how much something happens.

example.es: Por mucho que preguntes, no lo sé.
example.en: No matter how much you ask, I do not know.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a result stays true no matter how much something happens?
cards.answerEn: Use por mucho que, then a special verb form that leaves the amount or possibility open.
cards.noteEn: The special form is called the subjunctive. It often changes the ending: dicen becomes digan, and insistes becomes insistas. Por mucho que presents any amount of that action as unable to change the main result.

example.es: Por mucho que insistas, no cambiaré de opinión.
example.en: No matter how much you insist, I will not change my mind.

cards.answerEn: much; however much (in por mucho que)
cards.noteEn: Within por mucho que, mucho supplies the idea of an unrestricted amount or degree.

example.es: Por mucho que corra, llega tarde.
example.en: No matter how much he runs, he arrives late.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes por mucho que
cards.noteEn: Que links por mucho to the action whose amount does not change the result.

example.es: Por mucho que insistas, diré que no.
example.en: No matter how much you insist, I will say no.

cards.answerEn: to you all; you all (informal plural, used mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Os is the short object form used with vosotros or vosotras. It identifies several informally addressed people as receiving or being affected by an action.

example.en: I am sending you all a photo.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.answerEn: they tell you; people may tell you
cards.noteEn: After por mucho que, digan is a form of decir that leaves the amount or identity of what people say open. It is also the form used for a formal or plural command in other settings.

example.es: Por mucho que digan, mantendré mi decisión.
example.en: No matter what they say, I will keep my decision.

cards.questionEn: How do you tell a familiar group in Spain not to do something?
cards.answerEn: Put no or nunca before the negative command form for vosotros, such as no habléis or nunca salgáis.
cards.noteEn: Vosotros is the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain. For a regular -ar verb, replace -ar with -éis: hablar becomes habléis. For a regular -er or -ir verb, use -áis: comer becomes comáis and salir becomes salgáis, with some verbs also changing their stem.

example.es: No habléis todos a la vez.
example.en: Do not all speak at once.

cards.answerEn: stop; leave (command form for a familiar group)
cards.noteEn: Dejéis is the form used when telling more than one familiar person not to do something. In dejar de plus another action, dejar means to stop that action.

example.en: Do not stop practicing.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, then de, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form of a verb is called the infinitive. It usually ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only dejar changes to show who acts and when; the final verb stays in its dictionary form. Keep de in this pattern: dejar alone usually means “to leave” or “to let,” while dejar de + action means to stop doing that action.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone stops doing something?

example.en: I want to stop smoking.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links dejar to the activity being stopped
cards.noteEn: De is required between a form of dejar and the following action in the common pattern dejar de hacer algo, ‘to stop doing something.’

example.en: We stopped talking.

cards.promptEs: lotería · prueba viviente · sesgo de supervivencia
cards.questionEn: Why is the lottery winner's motivational advice misleading?
cards.answerEn: The visible winner treats persistence as proof while the many persistent losers are absent from the story.
cards.noteEn: This is survivorship bias: attention goes to the rare successful case that can give a talk, not to the much larger set of people who followed the same strategy and lost. The money bags make the speaker's luck visible, while the caption identifies the reasoning error.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.noteEn: Fracasado is the completed-action form of fracasar used after a form of haber.

example.en: The first attempt has failed.

cards.noteEn: In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

example.en: I tried it three times.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

example.en: I complain about the noise.

cards.noteEn: With a matching me, te, se, nos, or os marker, rendirse means to give up. Rendido is its completed-action form after haber.

example.en: I have not given up.

cards.noteEn: Empecé is the completed-past form of empezar used for yo. The spelling changes from z to c before é so the consonant sound stays the same.

example.en: I started reading yesterday.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone starts doing an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of empezar, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” The dictionary form, also called the infinitive, is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Empezar changes for the person and time; a stays fixed, and the action verb stays unchanged.

example.en: Lucía starts to read.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone works a scheduled shift?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of hacer followed by un turno or turnos.
cards.noteEn: Hacer changes for the person and time. Turno names the scheduled period of work; an adjective can specify its type, as in turno nocturno or turno doble.

example.es: Marta hace el turno de noche.
example.en: Marta works the night shift.

cards.noteEn: A turno is a scheduled period of work. Turnos is plural.

example.en: This week I am working three shifts.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.answerEn: double; twice as long or large
cards.noteEn: Dobles is plural because it describes more than one turno.

example.en: They worked two double shifts.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.en: We can enter now.

cards.noteEn: Billete can mean a ticket, banknote, or travel pass. With de lotería, it means a lottery ticket.

example.en: She bought two lottery tickets.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.noteEn: Veis is the present form of ver for informal plural vosotros, common in Spain.

example.en: Do you all see that light?

cards.noteEn: Prueba can mean a test, but it also means information or material that supports a claim.

example.es: Necesitamos una prueba de que ocurrió.
example.en: We need proof that it happened.

cards.questionEn: What expression describes a living person whose experience is presented as evidence?
cards.noteEn: Prueba names the evidence, and viviente emphasizes that a real living person embodies it. The expression does not by itself establish whether the evidence is reliable.

example.es: Ella es la prueba viviente de que se puede recuperar.
example.en: She is living proof that recovery is possible.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce the statement that some evidence supports?
cards.answerEn: Use prueba de que, followed by the statement.
cards.noteEn: Prueba names the evidence, de links it to its content, and que introduces a complete idea with its own verb.

example.es: Esta foto es prueba de que llegaron temprano.
example.en: This photo is proof that they arrived early.

cards.noteEn: Viviente has the same singular form with a masculine or feminine noun.

example.es: Es la persona viviente de mayor edad.
example.en: She is the oldest living person.

cards.answerEn: of; introducing what the evidence proves
cards.noteEn: After prueba, de can introduce the content supported by the evidence. When a whole statement follows, Spanish uses de que.

example.es: Hay pruebas de que el plan funciona.
example.en: There is evidence that the plan works.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what will happen if a real possibility occurs?
cards.answerEn: Use si with an ordinary present-time verb form for the condition, then state the result with a future form.
cards.noteEn: Si introduces a condition treated as genuinely possible. Spanish normally keeps the verb immediately after si in the present form, not the future. The result can use the future, built here by keeping the action verb and adding an ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.

example.en: If you finish early, we will have dinner together.

cards.answerEn: you all persevere; you all keep going
cards.noteEn: Perseveráis is the present form used with vosotros, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain.

example.en: If you all persevere, you will learn a lot.

cards.noteEn: Triunfaréis keeps the full verb triunfar and adds -éis for a future action by vosotros, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain.

example.en: With patience, you all will succeed.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

example.en: Marta will call tomorrow.

cards.noteEn: Charla can mean an informal conversation or a talk given to an audience. In the plural, charlas can refer to several presentations.

example.en: There will be two talks this afternoon.

cards.noteEn: Motivadoras uses feminine plural -as to match charlas.

example.en: We listened to some inspiring stories.

cards.answerEn: by; from (identifying the creator or source)
cards.noteEn: De can connect a work, statement, or piece of commentary to the person who created or supplied it. Natural English often uses “by” rather than literal “of.”

example.en: I read an article by Marta.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens successfully?
cards.answerEn: Use con éxito after the action.
cards.noteEn: Éxito means success. Together with con, the fixed phrase describes a successful outcome, much like the English word “successfully.” It does not change for person or time.

example.en: We completed the test successfully.

cards.noteEn: Deberían is a softened recommendation form of deber for a plural subject. It is followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: They should speak with her.

cards.promptEs: debería/deberías… + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone should do something?
cards.answerEn: Use an advice form of deber, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Use debería for “I,” “he,” “she,” or formal “you,” deberías for one familiar “you,” deberíamos for “we,” and deberían for a plural subject. The following action verb does not change.

example.en: We should rest.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

example.en: We would travel by train.

cards.noteEn: Avisar means making someone aware beforehand or notifying them.

example.en: You should warn us before entering.

cards.questionEn: What is the name for judging a process only from the visible successes while overlooking the failures?
cards.answerEn: Use sesgo de supervivencia for “survivorship bias.”
cards.noteEn: Sesgo means a systematic distortion in judgment. Supervivencia identifies the distortion: the cases that remain visible are easier to study than the cases that disappeared or failed, so success can look more common than it really is.

example.es: Estudiar solo las empresas exitosas crea un sesgo de supervivencia.
example.en: Studying only successful companies creates survivorship bias.
